summary:
Niskala is a web calendar that shows fire agencies in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, whether this month's fire hotspots are normal or not. NASA has recorded fire hotspots since 2000, but the record comes from two sensors that count differently: MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m). Simply adding them creates a fake jump in 2018, so the 20-year history cannot be trusted.

Niskala converts older MODIS counts to the VIIRS NOAA-20 scale with a separate ratio for each of the 14 districts, then compares every month with the same month in 2003–2025. Each month is colored from "much below normal" to "extreme" in a colorblind-safe calendar, with cards that answer when the season peaks, how bad this month is, and where it is worst. Results are checked against official SiPongi burned-area records (rank correlation 0.90). This helps district disaster agencies see an early or severe season as it starts.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Niskala is a harmonized hotspot anomaly calendar for West Kalimantan and its 14 districts. It answers one question for disaster agencies (BPBD): is this month's fire activity normal, and where is it unusual?

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Data: NASA FIRMS active fire data, MODIS C6.1 (Aqua) and VIIRS C2 (NOAA-20), 2001–2026. We keep vegetation fires, remove low-confidence and duplicate detections, assign each hotspot to a district, and count per month in local time.
  2. Harmonization: during the 2018–2025 overlap we learn how many NOAA-20 detections equal one Aqua detection in each district (5.3x for the province, 3.9x–8.3x by district). Small districts are pulled toward the province ratio. Older years are rescaled; from April 2018 NOAA-20 is used directly. A leave-one-year-out test shows district ratios cut the median error from 27.6% to 19.6%.
  3. Normal and anomaly: each month is divided by the mean of the same month in 2003–2025 (leaving out its own year) and placed in one of six classes.
  4. Validation: harmonized hotspots follow SiPongi burned area (Spearman 0.90, Pearson 0.93 at province level, 2016–2025). Years where burned area is much higher than hotspots suggest are flagged as possible hidden peat or smoke-covered fires.

WHAT USERS SEE

A year x month calendar (blue-white-red, colorblind-safe), three answer cards (When, How bad, Where), an interactive district map and ranking, area and date-range selection, CSV download of hotspots and monthly summaries, a printable PDF report, and full documentation with formulas.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

A province total can hide a district alarm: in July 2026 West Kalimantan was 1.4x normal, but Kayong Utara was already 8.3x normal, before its usual August peak. Niskala makes this visible in the same month, giving BPBD one consistent record to support readiness decisions. Because recent years already use VIIRS, the record continues when MODIS stops in 2027.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, Shapely, Jupyter) for the data pipeline; React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and KaTeX for the web app; hosted on Vercel. Code: https://github.com/sulthonaw/niskala

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Simple, explainable statistics that an agency can check; honest reporting of limits (hotspots are not burned area, smoke and smouldering peat can hide fires); and an experimental one-month forecast (Negative Binomial) that we keep separate because it under-predicts extreme seasons.
